case_name: State of Maharashtra v Narain Singh Yadav and another
respondent:
Narain Singh Yadav and another
Supreme Court of India

12 September 2002
Cr.As. Nos. 811-17 of 1995
The Order of the Court was as follows:
1.  Despite service, neither the respondents have filed vakalatnama nor put in appearance.
2.  The High Court at Bombay, in its writ jurisdiction u/art. 226 of the Constitution, thought it fit to quash the criminal proceedings solely on the ground of lapse of time.
3.  The decision in Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak 1991 Indlaw SC 313 stands considered in the latter pronouncement of this Court in P. Ramachandra Rao v. Union of India 1996 Indlaw SC 1996 Raj Deo Sharma v. State of Bihar 1998 Indlaw SC 1131 and Raj Deo Sharma (II) v. State of Bihar 1999 Indlaw SC 741 were stated to be no longer good laws. facts: The respondents have not filed vakalatnama nor put in appearance despite service.
The High Court at Bombay, in its writ jurisdiction u/art. 226 of the Constitution, thought it fit to quash the criminal proceedings solely on the ground of lapse of time.
This Court has had the opportunity to lay down certain specific guidelines in the matter of quashing of criminal complaints.

In P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka 2002 Indlaw SC 267 (supra) this Court observed: 'Secondly, though we are deleting the directions made respectively by two- and three-Judge Benches of this Court in the cases under reference, for reasons which we have already stated, we should not, even for a moment, be considered as having made a departure from the law as to speedy trial and speedy conclusion of criminal proceedings of whatever nature and at whichever stage before any authority or the court.'

The State cannot be permitted to deny the constitutional right of speedy trial to the accused on the ground that the State has no adequate financial resources to incur the necessary expenditure needed for improving the administrative and judicial apparatus with a view to ensuring speedy trial.

While considering the question of delay the court has a duty to see whether the prolongation was on account of any delaying tactics adopted by the accused and other relevant aspects which contributed to the delay.
issues: Whether the writ jurisdiction is available for quashing the criminal investigation unless there is error apparent on the face of the record or the proceedings can be termed to be mala fide in nature.

holding: The criminal appeals, thus, succeed. The order under appeal stands set aside. Criminal Cases Nos. 132/S, 133/S and 134/S of 1981 stand restored to the file of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 32nd Court, Esplanade, Bombay; Criminal Cases Nos. 12/S, 15/S, 17/S and 19/S of 1981, Criminal Cases Nos. 4/S, 5/S, 6/S, 7/S and 8/S of 1983 stand restored to the file of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, 38th Court, Ballard Pier, Bombay; and Sessions Case No. 446 of 1982 stands restored to the file of the Court of Session for Greater Bombay.
